# Flyology SIMD

Flyology SIMD is an experimental, standalone, strongly typed SIMD library for Ada.
It has zero runtime dependencies and does not define a Flyology parent package.

Canonical site: https://simd.flyology.org/
Guide: https://simd.flyology.org/guide/

Key constraints:
- The scalar backend defines public behavior.
- Public vector and mask representations are private.
- Lane zero is the first logical element loaded from memory.
- Partial loads and stores touch only the caller-declared valid extent.
- Primitive operations use compile-time backend selection.
- Runtime CPU dispatch occurs once at complete-array or whole-buffer algorithm boundaries.
- Runtime floating algorithms include binary32 and binary64 Sum and Dot_Product. Sum uses four binary32 or two binary64 accumulator groups; Dot_Product uses the same grouping after elementwise multiplication.
- Runtime byte algorithms include Find_First, Find_First_Of, Find_First_Difference, Equal, Count, and Is_ASCII. Find_First_Difference and Equal require identical array bounds and compare both complete buffers without reading beyond either tail.
- AArch64 NEON and x86-64 SSE2 implement the full 128-bit family.
- For operations without a separate Wide mechanism, the initial 256-bit Wide profile composes selected 128-bit operations or uses fixed-width Ada code on private parts. Wide Table_Lookup uses a target-selected lookup mechanism. AArch64 uses one two-register tbl operation for each result half. The composed x86-64 backend and a scalar build use one selected 128-bit Splat operation, four selected 128-bit Table_Lookup operations, two selected Subtract_Wrap operations, and two selected Bitwise_Or operations. The optional AVX2 backend uses one dedicated 256-bit implementation. Wide Compress and Expand use a target-selected compression and expansion mechanism.
- Wide supports one-source and two-source lane maps, bit casts between types with the same lane width and lane count, widening, narrowing, numeric conversion, 32-entry byte-table lookup, and an exact byte sum for U8x32.
- All 80 Wide Native memory overloads compose selected 128-bit operations. Full, unaligned, and aligned forms call the matching operation for both private parts. Partial loads and stores choose selected full and partial operations from Count. When Count does not exceed the private lane count, a partial load uses selected Zero for the high part. A scalar build uses the same composition through the portable 128-bit implementation.
- On AArch64, Wide Compress and Expand apply selected 128-bit To_Bit_Mask to both private mask parts and combine the compact results. The mechanism derives one 32-byte index map and runs one two-register TBL operation for each 128-bit result half. The x86-64 composed and AVX2 mechanisms each derive one two-source lane map for each 128-bit result half. Each mechanism calls selected 128-bit Permute_Lanes twice and selected 128-bit Select_Value twice. Select_Value selects Zero for each zero-fill lane.
- Wide Native integer Reduce_Add_Wrap, Reduce_Min, and Reduce_Max reduce both private parts with selected 128-bit reductions. The implementation splats each scalar result, combines the two vectors with selected 128-bit Add_Wrap, Min, or Max, and extracts lane zero. This grouping is valid because the three integer operations are associative.
- Wide Native floating Reduce_Add, Reduce_Min_Number, and Reduce_Max_Number combine lanes in ascending lane order and do not reduce the private parts independently. Reduce_Add starts from positive zero. The minimum-number and maximum-number reductions start from lane zero. On AArch64, dedicated Advanced SIMD sequences perform scalar fadd, fminnm, or fmaxnm operations in ascending lane order. The x86-64 composed and AVX2 selections use dedicated SSE2 leaves that process lanes in ascending order. A scalar build uses the portable Wide implementation.
- The Wide lane-movement operations are Reverse_Lanes, both slide operations, both interleave operations, and both deinterleave operations. These operations and both Permute_Lanes overloads use a target-selected permutation mechanism. The AArch64 backend uses one TBL operation with a two-register table per result half for reverse, slides, and the one-source overload. It uses one TBL operation with a four-register table per result half for interleave, deinterleave, and the two-source overload. On composed x86-64, reverse and the one-source overload call selected 128-bit two-source Permute_Lanes twice. Interleave, deinterleave, and the two-source overload call selected 128-bit two-source Permute_Lanes four times and selected Select_Value twice to choose between the two sources. Slides call selected 128-bit two-source Permute_Lanes twice and selected Select_Value twice against Zero. The optional AVX2 implementation uses 256-bit byte shuffles and cross-half selection.
- An x86-64 build can statically select isolated AVX2-specific 256-bit implementations for U8x32 and I8x32 wrapping, saturating, bitwise, minimum, and maximum operations, plus U8x32 Table_Lookup. Each byte comparison and Select_Value uses a relation-specific isolated leaf. The Less_Than leaf reverses the operands of its greater-than comparison. The Less_Equal leaf complements that comparison with the original operand order. The Greater_Equal leaf complements it with reversed operands.
- The same static AVX2 selection uses isolated 256-bit Add, Subtract, Multiply, Divide, Min_Number, and Max_Number implementations for F32x8 and F64x4. Floating arithmetic uses one packed operation. Minimum and maximum use integer classification and bit selection to preserve the public NaN and signed-zero rules. The composed x86-64 and AArch64 backends use two selected 128-bit operations.
- The Wide AVX2 backend requires FLYOLOGY_SIMD_ARCH=x86_64 and FLYOLOGY_SIMD_AVX2=enabled. It has no runtime feature gate. On each deployment target, CPUID must report the AVX, AVX2, and OSXSAVE bits, and XCR0 must enable XMM and YMM register state.
- The optional complete-array and whole-buffer AVX2 entry points check CPU and OS extended state before they call AVX2 objects.
- No low-level operation allocates, performs I/O, locks, waits, or starts a task.
- The project initially requires GCC-based GNAT and remains experimental.
